Fermi's Paradox breaks down in the last two points.

It's true that sol is a pretty common type of star. Given the number of stars, it's not unreasonable that there could be life-bearing planets around other stars.

Here's where it utterly breaks down:

Might. Skipping lightly over the fact that both the theory and engineering behind interstellar travel has stymied the best and brightest we have to offer. Warning- sleep deprived ramblings below:

My own take is that there is simply too much space between civilizations. I'd like to think that someday we will develop faster than light travel, but honestly I have doubts as to the feasibility of doing so. Even at light speed it would take years for us to get to our nearest neighboring stars let alone the nearest habitable worlds.

I suppose it is possible that there is other intelligent life out there that is not based on carbon (or is anything even remotely what we would expect of advanced civilizations) that would be closer than a few dozen light years. I suspect that the chances of our being able to communicate with them would be slim at best, something along the lines of an ant communicating with a worm.

I think life is rarer and harder to form than we currently take it to be. Even if a planet has absolutely perfect conditions to harbor some form of life there's absolutely no guarantee that life will be there.

Furthermore, even if there is life on these planets, based upon what we've witnessed here on earth it takes billions of years to even get to the point that we're currently at. It's not unreasonable at all to believe that there is an abundance of human-like life in the (relatively) near vicinity of earth which is a few evolutionary steps behind us. To us, seeing a Neanderthal-equivalent of some other species may seem disappointing, but think of how many billions of years it took life to get to that point. In a "percentage of completion" way of thinking, they would be very close to us. Shoot, we only developed the ability to send and receive radio signals in the past couple of centuries, what if there are many civilizations that are essentially still in the 1700's.

I apply Occam's razor. There are no alien civilizations out there. I suspect the great filter is that Jupiter like planets have a high likelihood of clearing the inner habitable orbits in the vast majority of systems (that our system layout is rather rare).

People really don't have a sense of scale when it comes to the size of the universe and, more importantly, time. The Milky Way is very, very big and very, very old. We've all seen the infographics showing just how infinitesimally small a fraction of time humanity has existed compared to the rest of life on earth, or the universe in general. Seriously - we have been using radio for 100 years, but have existed as a species for a period of time 1000 times that long. We have big imaginations but a critically small frame of reference.

Even in a conservative estimate of the Fermi Paradox, which says that there should be a double-digit count of advanced civilizations in our galaxy at this point, even if we all existed at some point the odds of us existing simultaneously are slim to none. Do civilizations survive tens of thousands of years? Would they be recognizable as life?

And then there's distance. Even if you had, say, four civilizations evenly spread throughout the galaxy, they'd be 150,000 lightyears apart! We haven't even existed as a species long enough to even see light from when their evolutionary ancestors were on the planet, let alone actually contact them! Given the number of stars in the galaxy, and the fact that we can't actually contact each other, the odds of ever coming into contact is... slim to none.

But let's assume that a radically advanced civilization appeared before us in time, and long enough ago that it had a chance to spread throughout the galaxy - thereby avoiding the problem of time and distance. Here, the problem is - would we even recognize life if we saw it? We have a grand sample size of one when it comes to life - carbon-based, ribonucleic-chemistry life suited for life on a warm, wet, rocky world with a circular orbit. We have a grand sample size of one when it comes to technology - we see high technology as utilization of electromagnetism for communication and information storage, with "radio" and "integrated circuits" being our standard for tech levels.

Would we even be able to recognize, say, a silicon-based lifeform that used optical computing or, worse, didn't use computing at all? Would we be able to detect a civilization using technology other than radio, or had technology so advanced that it'd be to us as our radio is to an ant? XKCD is relevant as always. It's a matter of stupid pride, on our part - we assume that, being the most advanced species on our planet, we'd be able to recognize the most advanced species of any other planet, right? Yeah, not a chance - even now, we're becoming a Fermi Ghost because we've stopped using radio communications on a large scale, with most of our data and information moving to fiber optics and lasers!

The Fermi Paradox asks "If life is common, why don't we see it?" The solution isn't "There isn't as much life as we think," the solution is "The sandbox is beyond our ability to scale."

I find the Fermi Paradox leaves out a very important factor which must be considered. The speed of light. (This might alleviate some of that existential crisis)

Consider that SETI has only been functional since 1960. We have been broadcasting radio waves into space since almost exactly 100 years ago. Do you know how far those radio waves have reached till now? Take a peek.

Seriously. We have announced our capabilities as a technological and sentient species to such a tiny tiny fragment of a fraction of the galaxy (let alone the universe as a whole). Also consider that we no longer broadcast as much as we used to into space. Using the ionosphere to bounce off radio waves is OLD tech. Almost nobody uses that anymore.

So essentially, we spent about 50-60 years being a radio-noisy planet (in a fairly limited frequency range) and we expect advanced civilizations to rush to us and roll out a red carpet? It's the equivalent of a teenager on youtube uploading five videos about how terrible her day at school was, stopping uploading for a month, and then wondering why she isn't getting thousands of likes and turning into the next Beiber.

To be noticed, we would need alien life forms to be looking in the right direction, in the right frequency range, and be well within range of that 200 light-year bubble. Either that, or we would need to be patient and stop giving up before we've barely started. The light-year problem extends the other way too. Alien civilizations may be swarming over vast tracts of our milky way for far longer than ten thousand years, and we might not be aware of it because the milky way itself is over one hundred thousand light-years in diameter. So the further we see into space, the further back we are seeing into time as well. The images we get from the opposite side of the galaxy are 100,000 years old. To give you some sense of time, 100,000 years ago, humans as a species was just beginning to crawl out of Africa. We had no concept of agriculture or anything of the sort. Proper agriculture was 90,000 years AFTER that. Look at all we've achieved in 10,000 years, and that is despite stuff like the dark ages setting us back 2000 years mysticism and superstition and other stupid hurdles. In the time that light takes to travel to us from just outside our local neighborhood, entire alien civilizations could rise up, die, and rise anew. But the Fermi-Paradox writes all of this off so easily.

Looking at our 200 light-year bubble again. There are only about 500 G-type stars in this bubble. As of 2005, we had only found planets around 28 of them. I'm sure we have found a whole bunch more since then, but even then, we are just BEGINNING to probe at space.

It is far too early to feel despair. It is far too early to let defeatist concepts like the Fermi Paradox guide our understanding of our universe.

Well first of all it isn't a paradox. A paradox has a logical contradiction and most paradox's that people think of aren't actually paradox's. Allow me to quote Richard Feynmann: "the 'paradox' is only a conflict between reality and your feeling of what reality 'ought'"

Just because there is a high probabilty that there are alien species doesn't imply that we should have had contact. There are a ton of different reasons why we would never have had contact that are more likely than not:

  • They don't communicate on a spectrum that we look at. Ex. they could use gamma radiation the way we use light (the visible spectrum).

  • Their civilization hasn't intersected with ours time wise. The closest start is really really really really really really really far away and other are even further.

I have seriously considered that we where already visited a long time ago. I don't think it's any coincidence that human religions started out as animistic-Earth centered beliefs and ended up obsessed with the sky and eternally chasing powerful observers that we think live there. Many cultures have stories of wars among celestials that were looking to usurp control of earth with humans stuck in the middle and powerless to intervene.Some event must have been the inspiration for all these myths.

The thing that mostly occurs to me is that expansion is incredibly exponential:

  • 500 years ago we were celebrating crossing an ocean.
  • 130 years ago we were celebrating the first car engine.
  • 110 years ago we were celebrating the first airplane flight.
  • 50 years ago we put the first man on the moon.
  • 3 years ago Voyager became the first man made object to travel outside our solar system and on into interstellar space.

Humanity by all accounts is a young race in an old solar system. Other species had head starts in the millions to billions of years. If we can go from cheering about crossing an ocean to crossing into another solar system in 500 years, can you even fathom what we'll be doing in a million years? A billion years? Expanding across the universe is so banal a prediction that it goes without saying. Yet here we are, in a universe that's been here for billions of years before us and it seems nobody has managed to do that, or frankly much of anything, so far as we can tell.

The extermination event theory, such that intelligent life eventually yet inevitably eradicates itself when reaching a sufficient level of technology (through weaponry, planetary/environmental destruction, etc), seems compelling yet suffers from the fact that there would be relics. We're already sending objects outside our solar system. Self replicating robotic probes, or Von Neumann probes, are an inevitability and may very well happen within our lifetimes. The idea there is a machine capable of building a machine that builds more of itself. These probes find a distant body with sufficient mineral deposits for reproduction -perhaps a planet, moon, or even a comet. They then setup a factory and produce however many more of these probes which then in turn go set out in different directions with the same goal - all while sending information back home. It would result in an exponential growth of these probes that would eventually end up scattered more or less everywhere in the universe.

Of the many possibilities I think the most probable is one that also sounds the most outlandish at first - that we're living in a simulation. There's actually a very compelling and simple logical argument for this. We're already developing virtual reality technology and while it's certainly extremely primitive there is 0 doubt that some time, even if hundreds or thousands of years from now, we'll be able to develop immersive technology that can replicate something that can pass as a universe. I don't think anybody would really argue against this, yet the incredibly bizarre thing is that if this is true then it's logically almost a certainty that we're already living in a simulation. At the point any species develops this technology realities will begin to fork. There will be an infinite number of possible simulations running for any number of reasons- pleasure, entertainment, education, training, perhaps even punitive measures. And some simulations themselves may go on to develop more simulations. Yet there will be only one 'real' universe. If you take any given reality the odds it's the real reality become ever closer to 0.

And there has been an enormous amount of scientific effort put into considering and testing this possibility. For instance a variety of teams at the US Department of Energy's Fermilab have been at it for years. Here are some selected articles from them. Nick Bostrom, an influence on many including Elon Musk, has a page setup here with a wide array of material available on the topic as well. Definitely a fun question. That article from WaitButWhy is just incredible and I think is going to be outlook changing for anybody who reads it but hasn't seriously considered these questions before.
